div.p: OUR FUTURE POLICY IN TILE EAST

Tiffs"' is a lull in the sphere of polities just now. A stormy time may supervene; in. deed the over-eharged atmosphere must soon relieve itself, unless the -laws which regulate the growth and condition the activity of the social organism are to be falsiied and the national character for con- sistency is to suffer irretrievable shock. It will not long suit the humour of those

that British interests should make a brave show in diplomatic correspondence, and he Trotted out on every available occasion of I state ceremony. The bulk of the people, Thou Fla they may not be so clever as the politicians to whom they uonfide their des- tinies, have an awkward habit of entering Into judgment with them when they suspect That they have been humbugged. If analogy be not an unreliable guide, and history worthless for purposes of moral in- struction, the living generation will require • strict amount at the hands of our settle?. • and blundering leaders, who have contrived to throw away the grandest chances of Eastern pacification. As to the verdict of posterity, are Tories themselves so bigotted and infatuated as to doubt that it will go against the feeble and divided adrainistra- . don which Lord Beaconsfield rules? Meanwhile the business of life goes on, though not without travail and uncertainty which might have been avoided. The winter draws nigh, and trade does not brighten. How can it when Europe threatens to become a vast camp and markets are closing? Paying the Khedive's debte, and fitting out mercenary legion. to war on the side of the Turk, may be as entertaining as cockfighting, but they hardly rank with the productive industries of the time. There is a tide in Ihe affairs of nations as well as of men, and our rulers have let it go past. We are not of the number of those who thii4 that Governments can do and prevent what- ever they please, but our late foreign policy has illustrated the terrific and far-reaching result of stateamanship devoid of genius more signally than any English policy since the American War of Independence. We may learn to forgive the injury to our credit; we cannot easily forget the havoc wrought in the plains of the Danube. That the of Lies should labour in and out of goggogi,,.; sully a great and spotless name is not such a great thing after all. That cynics should set highe: store on bond-holding claim, than on those of oppressed and out- raged peasants in itulgana is not to be wondered at either. But that the traditional eupportere of a National Eriligion (?) should have lacked the faith and oeurage which the ' crisis demauded, and let slip the dogs of wan I rather than accept the moral support of the Liberal party may well fill us, as it has done Mr. Gladstone, 'with shame and astonish- ment." The question is constantly ruing to men's lips, and it must soon be answered— What is the Government prepared to do should the battle be a drawn one, and dis- ease and famine combine with bad general- ship to defeat the .dussian purpose. Of 'course, it is barely supposable that the Turks • will have it all their own way; but they I may wear out the seal and endurance of the ' Cur and his Generals. At all event., we aught to be on the alert whenever the negotiations begin. We cannot undo the past, but we may do something to mitigate or prevent the evils which will certainly again arise if huseiao championship of , the oppressed nationalities prove a eon,. parative failure. If we don't do it, it will— we rejoice to believe—be done by other hands. It cannot be that the miscreants who have cursed those fair and fruitful provinees with their polluting presence should be reinsteted m their tyrannical and rapicious dominion. The conseutaneous voice of the civilised world has already declared that such mime and scandal must not again flourish unchecked. Let our leaders prepare to do their duty. It they . would do something to redeem past errors, and snatch a little credit for genuine , patriotism, while • few grains of sand yet remain in the hour glints, let them throw off I I the ardour of Machiavellian subtlety in which they have been entangled by their cm/vastly chief, and go out to conquer the giant difficulty in the strength et truth, humanity, and righteousness. After all that callous hearts have urged, the golden rule remaine true—true for nations as for individuals. Justice is the true cement of civilisation. No bond is so strong and enduring as a generous care for one another; no interests worthy of a moment's considera- tion can outweigh the demands of equity. When the motto ol our rulers is again, "Be just, and fear not," when we have learned to look not on our own things merely, but also on the things of other., then shall our light shine out of the present obscurity, and • regenerated laud—inhabited by a grateful and freedom-loving race—may yet divide Russian from lurk, and insensibly modify their national characteristics for good. Tur- key herself, warned by costly experience, may then take a leaf out of the book of civiiiratiou, and the baptism of blood and are not have been utterly in vain.

Penge tragedy is receding into the viata of the poet, and the verdict recorded against the act, re in it is the domestic Demotion of the hour, Some of the London papers have allowed the subject to ho debated in their columns; and borristers, medical men, and others, have freely canvassed the long and eloquent (" sadly too eloquent" say the critical) summing up of Mr. Justice Hawkins and the finding of the jury. Now, the fact that the old superstitious veneration for judicial decisions is becoming rare, and that ex cathedra utterances are no more deemed infallible in a court of law than they are in a Church Congress, or an Ecumenical Council, or a Methodist Con- _ . .

forum, does not seem to us to be In itself lamentable. Unbelief is always the shaded side of a larger belief ; implies, in fact, an affirmation of its contrary. People know 'that the wisest make mistakes ; still, they Ido not disparage wisdom. In the present instance, the convergence of many lines of circumstantial evidence towards the conclu- sion that, if starving and ill-treatment be murder, murder :las been committed, seems to have made the duty of the jury easier than many allow themselves to think it was. Then again, the notion that a judge has only to gather up and enumerate the various items of evidence; that, in fact, he ought to abstain from letting his own judgment peep through, and even from emphasizing those crucial points which supply the elements of a sound decision, is absurd. He cannot free himself from grave responsibility; for, though the jury have the matter in their own hands, he is entrusted with the solemn right to hold up ' the balances before them, and weigh the evidence for and against a conviction. Specially is this true of a case so complex, and one requiring no firm a grasp, and so clear mid trained an intelligence as this. The outburst of sentiment in fair of the accused is not, however, really based upon a belief in their innocence. It in due to the rising disgust of cultivated minds and hearts against death by hanging. The gallows is a relic of barbaric ages. A long and patient trial—fenced round by the sealous safe- guards of a " legal " system which has been devised mainly for the protection of mourn. Now patiently tracking the course of scientific experiment through its ancient and modern windings, and then mounting of the wings of a richly endowed imagination to the realms of the future and unseen, the Profaner claimed the rapt at- tention on his audience, and must have won their admiration for his ability and candour, I even when they shrank from adopting his 1 conclusions.
